summary: The runtime's replay guarantee holds and is genuinely falsifiable. run_simulation.py:93 replays the ledger read back from disk (trace.read_ledger), not the live in-memory list; all 21 completed runs report exact=true, llm_calls=0, empty ledger_integrity and non-zero checked counts, and I independently re-derived state_hash, event ids, integrity and checked counts from each on-disk ledger.jsonl and they agree with every stored value. I confirmed the check can fail: against a live world, rewriting a committed event, forging an actor decision, flipping the terminal, rewiring a cause, forging a timestamp, deleting every semantic.world_call, truncating the ledger and a near-empty ledger are all caught (the earlier REPLAY_DETERMINISM_REVIEW.md headline that a forged ledger is certified exact does not reproduce on the current code). Determinism is clean (no random/uuid/datetime.now/time.time in the runtime or kernel; total event order (t, depth, seq); identical replay digests under PYTHONHASHSEED 0/1/12345), deep copies are used and provably mutate neither the live world nor the input, and every event id is exactly e{seq} with all sources, call ids and trajectory ids code-owned across all 21 ledgers. As a stronger check than the system performs on itself, replaying every ledger prefix reproduced 198/198 persisted actor prompts. My findings are all MEDIUM or LOW: the offline re-verification helper reports an 'exact' verdict it never computes, the disk round-trip has no test at all, the actor prompt's why-now line is not in the ledger, and the ledger is held only in memory until the run ends.

findings.title: evaluation/reverify_replay.py prints exact=True for ledgers it never verified
findings.evidence: evaluation/reverify_replay.py:34-35 copies `exact` verbatim out of the run's existing replay_verification.json instead of deriving it, and :53 then prints it on the same CLI line as the freshly-derived calls/events/integrity. Demonstrated on scratchpad copies of artifacts/matched_pairs/c1_against_stereotype: with a committed event rewritten to "Ethel gives up and calls her grandson to do it for her.", with the final semantic.terminal_check flipped from YES to NO_AT_CUTOFF, with a journal.event cause rewired to seq 2, and with the second half of the ledger deleted, the tool prints `ok <name> exact=True calls=0 integrity=ok` for all four and exits 0. evaluation/verify_run.py:97-98 has the same shape ('replay was not exact' is decided by reading replay["exact"] out of the file). The ok predicate at reverify_replay.py:49-50 also omits `vacuous` and never looks at terminals, so the half-deleted ledger (16 events, no terminal record) still reports ok.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the tool an independent party is pointed at to re-check the strongest claim in the system, and it emits a verdict it did not compute in a format indistinguishable from one it did; --write would then bake that unverified `exact: true` back into a tampered run's replay_verification.json. Every currently stored file is genuine (all 21 carry the full nine-key live-world comparison set, all true, and none carries the exact_verified_against tag), so no artifact is actually wrong today — but the check offers no protection against one being wrong tomorrow.
findings.suggested_fix: Print the carried value as `exact(from run, not re-derived)` or drop it from the CLI line entirely, and fold `vacuous` and terminal presence into the ok predicate.

findings.title: No test covers the persisted-file path; the 'replay from disk' guarantee has no regression guard
findings.evidence: `grep -rn "read_ledger|write_artifacts|run_simulation" tests/` returns nothing. Every replay test — tests/test_semantic_runtime.py:656, :668, :1047 and tests/test_compiler_runtime_integration.py:120 — calls replay_trajectory(world.records, live_world=world) on the live in-memory list. The disk round-trip exists only at run_simulation.py:90-93 and is exercised by no test. The full suite is 247 passed.
findings.why_it_matters: replay.py:1-12 and run_simulation.py:87-89 both state that replaying the in-memory list 'would only prove the process can talk to itself', yet reverting run_simulation.py:93 to replay_trajectory(world.records, live_world=world) would leave all 247 tests green. The single property the module exists to establish is the one property nothing guards.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a test that runs a scripted trajectory, calls write_artifacts into tmp_path, replays read_ledger(tmp_path) and asserts exact — and that editing one byte of the written ledger.jsonl makes it non-exact.

findings.title: The actor prompt is not fully determined by the ledger, and views_match compares one end-state view per actor rather than the views actually shown
findings.evidence: views.py:42 takes trigger_event_ids and views.py:62-65 turns them into the 'WHAT HAS CHANGED SINCE YOUR LAST TURN' block; trajectory.py:433 passes them, but the semantic.actor_call record written at trajectory.py:477-481 stores only call_id, actor, decision, intentions and trajectory_id. Replaying every ledger prefix up to each of the 198 semantic.actor_call records across all 21 runs reproduces the persisted prompt exactly for 148 and diverges on 50 in exactly that block — e.g. artifacts/simulations_v3/case1_cold_email call c6, on disk '- you observed: Jordan Reyes sends the cold email to Mark Cuban's public email address.' vs from the ledger '- time has passed and you are looking at your situation again'. Separately, replay.py:117-118 builds views as one build_view() per actor at the END state with no trigger ids, so those 198 prompts are never compared, though replay.py:23 claims 'every actor's whole view'.
findings.why_it_matters: Not a leak — the block is composed only from events that actor demonstrably observed, and the real prompts are persisted in actor_views.jsonl — but the authoritative record does not determine the model's input, nothing cross-checks actor_views.jsonl against the ledger, and the self-check's wording overstates its coverage.
findings.suggested_fix: Record trigger_event_ids in the semantic.actor_call record and reconstruct the historical views in _projection instead of only the end-state ones.

findings.title: The ledger is held only in memory until the run ends, and three kernel exceptions escape run_trajectory
findings.evidence: run_simulation.py:90 -> trace.py:48 is the only write of ledger.jsonl and happens after run_trajectory returns; there is no incremental flush (World.dump_ledger is never called by the runtime). trajectory.py:963-967 catches EnvelopeError, ActorGroundingError, EventGroundingError, RuntimeTechnicalFailure and ValueError, plus CallBudgetExceeded at :949. WorldIntegrityError, SchedulingInPastError and ZeroTimeLoopError are all RuntimeError subclasses, not ValueError (verified by issubclass), so any of them — or a KeyboardInterrupt — propagates out of main() and the entire ledger of a paid-for run is lost. trace.py:33 also opens ledger.jsonl with mode 'w' and streams, so a crash mid-write leaves a truncated authoritative record with no original to fall back on.
findings.why_it_matters: The same concern is explicitly handled elsewhere — trace.py:31-32 says 'an artifact write happens after a whole paid-for run, and must never be the thing that loses it' — but only for encoding errors. An unexpected kernel exception loses the whole record, which is exactly the failure the ledger is supposed to be immune to. Not observed in any of the 21 runs; every cause passed in trajectory.py is a previously returned seq and every scheduled instant is >= clock.now, so these paths are latent rather than live.
findings.suggested_fix: Write ledger.jsonl from a finally block (or incrementally), to a temp file in the same directory followed by os.replace.

findings.title: check_ledger_integrity accepts a record that names itself as its own cause
findings.evidence: replay.py:57 adds the current seq to `seqs` before the cause membership test at replay.py:72, so cause == seq passes. Demonstrated on a copy of artifacts/matched_pairs/c1_against_stereotype: setting seq 11's cause to 11 yields zero integrity problems, while setting it to 16 correctly reports "seq 11 names a cause 16 that does not exist before it". replay.py:19 claims the check enforces 'every cause existing and preceding its record'.
findings.why_it_matters: A self-caused record is a broken causal chain that the one check whose entire purpose is to be capable of failing would certify as sound. Unreachable from the runtime's own call sites today, so the exposure is to a future call site or a tampered ledger rather than to current behaviour.
findings.suggested_fix: Test `cause` against the set of seqs seen before adding the current record's own seq.
